4369e5a1d2532ff1.summary: Syria textbook controversy deepens distrust in government newspress_en Thu, 11/12/2026 - 03:30 Opinion Syria’s school textbooks have come under intense scrutiny after comparisons between editions revealed altered illustrations of women, removed historical material and missing lessons on citizenship. Much of the debate has focused on what these changes mean for children’s education. Far less attention has been paid to an equally troubling issue: the Education Ministry’s…

ai.sum: Syria's school textbook revisions, including altered images of women and removed content, have deepened public distrust in the government.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Syrian textbook controversy is less about the content changes themselves than about the Education Ministry's handling of it. Comparing editions revealed altered illustrations of women (headscarves added), modified images of ancient sculptures, and deleted lessons on citizenship and local administration. The ministry's 26 October statement framed the revisions as removing former-regime propaganda and denied changes after January 2025, but the authors contend this explanation does not cover many of the documented alterations. They say the ministry focused on timing rather than motive, left unexplained why disputed material escaped review before nationwide distribution, and so failed a test of accountability for a transitional government. The piece accepts that removing Assad-era propaganda was necessary but rejects replacing it with another set of social preferences.
brief.argument: The Education Ministry's evasive response to documented textbook alterations, which exceed its stated aim of removing Assad-era propaganda, is deepening distrust in the transitional government.
recommendations: Give credible educational justifications for each alteration rather than relying on the Assad-legacy explanation.
Explain why the disputed material was not adequately reviewed before textbooks were distributed nationwide.
Restore or justify the removal of civic lessons on rights, responsibilities and public participation.

ai.sum: Al Majalla's film column reviews recent films, including Lee Chang-dong's Possible Love.

brief.summary: This is a film review column from Al Majalla covering four or five recent releases in Arab and regional cinema. The authors praise Lee Chang-dong's Possible Love for its patient, psychologically layered examination of class, inequality and the ethics of turning a community's suffering into art. They describe Dancing Angels as a debut thriller-drama about a teenager crushed by family and school violence, The Blind Ferryman as a poetic Iraqi marsh-set love story with a strong visual sense, Bakma as a Tunisian horror film using violence and childhood trauma to probe criminal behaviour, and Berleen as an interwoven ensemble drama about Arab migrants in Berlin. The column reads each work through its themes and craft rather than advancing a policy argument.
brief.argument: The column argues that these recent films, from Korea, Türkiye, Iraq, Tunisia and Egypt, are notable for their treatment of social inequality, trauma and authoritarian control, and for their distinctive authorial styles.
brief.turkey: Dancing Angels, a Türkiye-Croatia co-production by Ferit Kılıç set in Istanbul, is the only title with a direct Turkish link, and the review treats it as a critique of violence imposed on children under family and school authority.

Technology has made it easier for anyone to access military know-how, triggering a policy debate on how to constrain non-state actors in the digital space. For their part, the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in…

ai.sum: Analysis examines how generative AI gives non-state actors access to specialised military and cyber know-how.

brief.summary: The authors argue that generative AI gives non-state armed groups access to specialised technical know-how across missile engineering, simulation, cyber operations and drone swarms, lowering barriers that once required state resources. Their main evidence is an Anthropic report on a Houthi-linked cell that used a commercial model in place of human engineers to diagnose a failed rocket test, build offline simulation software after its accounts were banned, and pursue several weapons programmes. The piece adds a Cambridge study finding AI units inside Boko Haram-linked factions, though it did not measure any effect on strike capability, and a Century Foundation study showing Houthi weapons increasingly assembled locally from imported Chinese and Iranian components. The authors suggest the cases are likely the visible tip of a wider trend and call for policy debate on constraining non-state actors' use of AI.
brief.argument: Commercially available generative AI is enabling non-state armed groups to advance missile, drone and cyber capabilities, shifting weapons production toward decentralised local assembly.

It presents China as balancing two positions: upholding freedom of navigation while recognising the Aden government in Yemen, and negotiating directly with the Houthis and Iran for safe passage of its tankers. It notes that China has been upgrading its Djibouti base since 2024, but cites a Chinese commentator who says this does not signal a bigger military presence or a challenge to Western alliances. The authors also link the Somaliland question, after Trump's remarks and Israel's diplomatic moves, to the strategic weight of the Bab al-Mandab. A 2026 memorandum under Xi's Global Security Initiative is presented as a framework for maritime and counter-terror cooperation that may help Djibouti avoid regional entanglement.
brief.argument: China is expanding its security and diplomatic coordination with Djibouti to protect its maritime interests in the Red Sea without necessarily expanding its military footprint.

54d20e95d6d91326.title: The Promise of Biomanufacturing at the Edge
54d20e95d6d91326.summary: As the old adage goes, “Amateurs talk strategy. Professionals talk logistics.” Military operations are utterly dependent on complex supply chains to move food, fuel, and other essential products across long distances and through contested environments to reach the warfighter. These vital supply lines are fragile at every stage: production concentrated in a single facility can be disrupted, key inputs may come from unreliable — or adversarial — foreign suppliers, and the…

ai.sum: A War on the Rocks article argues that biomanufacturing at the tactical edge could reduce military supply chain fragility.

brief.summary: The authors argue that US military supply lines are fragile, and that forward-deployed biomanufacturing, engineered microbes turning simple feedstocks into fuels, chemicals, plastics or food, could cut that dependence by producing materials near the front. Unlike fixed plants, one bioreactor platform can be reprogrammed across products, which suits hard-to-forecast demand. They note early prototypes (a containerised Naval Research Laboratory unit, DARPA-backed food and beach-binding programmes) and that many firms each hold one piece of the solution. Their case is that no market will assemble these pieces into deployable systems, so the Pentagon must coordinate the firms, run a dedicated demonstration programme, and name end-users early to create a path to procurement. They also flag regulatory questions and say the technology is not yet mature enough to field.
brief.argument: Forward-deployed biomanufacturing can make US forces less dependent on vulnerable supply chains, but only if the Pentagon deliberately integrates fragmented firms and builds a clear route from prototype to procurement.
recommendations: Bring together the specialised companies under existing consortium structures such as the Defense Industrial Base Consortium.
Establish a dedicated programme within the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering to demonstrate deployable systems and manage technology transition.
Engage logistics customers early, including US Transportation Command, the Defense Logistics Agency and Naval Supply Systems Command, to define needs and commit to offtake.
Work with regulators such as the EPA and FDA to clarify regulatory treatment of military biomanufacturing applications.

brief.argument: Arab parties' record 19 seats gave Eisenkot the mandate, but their divided positions and conditions for support will limit how far that electoral clout translates into policy influence.

a416fb8df0930980.title: Seeking the source: Biological attribution from anthrax to AI
a416fb8df0930980.summary: Attribution can be imprecise, since it oftentimes relies on a combination of science, intelligence, and investigatory evidence. The post Seeking the source: Biological attribution from anthrax to AI appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council article discusses how biological weapons attacks are attributed, from anthrax to AI.

brief.summary: The authors argue that AI can already help design novel biological threats, possibly ones that evade current attribution methods, so attribution capability must advance in step. They note that US attribution has improved since the 2001 anthrax attacks but remains unready for the next biological attack. Knowing whether an event was natural, accidental or deliberate shapes law enforcement, intelligence and White House responses, and mistaken accusations carry diplomatic and security costs. Responsibility is spread across the FBI, DHS, HHS and the intelligence community, and the authors say the current arrangement has not unified these elements to get findings to decision-makers in time. They call for procedures, protocols and information-sharing mechanisms to be in place before an event, covering evidence collection, evaluation of competing explanations, and clear evidentiary thresholds for attributing responsibility.
brief.argument: The US must build a unified, pre-established biological attribution capability, with AI as a tool, because AI-enabled threats could outpace current methods.
recommendations: Establish attribution procedures, protocols and information-sharing mechanisms before a biological event occurs.
Cover the full attribution chain: evidence collection, evaluation of competing explanations, and communication of conclusions.
Define the evidentiary and intelligence thresholds needed before judging responsibility for a biological event.
Use AI to strengthen attribution capacity as AI-enabled threat design advances.

1de039446674dc4d.title: What the Abu Dhabi Talks Did—and Didn’t—Achieve
1de039446674dc4d.summary: Trilateral talks on the war in Ukraine ended without a breakthrough. CFR experts weigh in on the results and where negotiations might go next.

ai.sum: Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on the Ukraine war ended without a breakthrough, according to CFR experts.

brief.summary: The piece is a roundup of CFR experts on the Abu Dhabi trilateral talks between US, Russian and Ukrainian negotiators, which ended without a breakthrough but produced an agreed-in-principle prisoner exchange. Liana Fix argues that widening talks to European security gives Europeans a seat at the table but lets Russia delay a sectoral ceasefire and could leave Europe vulnerable. Matthias Matthijs sees no real progress, arguing Europeans lack a single representative and that Washington's quasi-neutral stance means the war may last two more years. Max Boot calls the talks a waste of time that legitimises the Kremlin, urging more support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia. Thomas Graham argues the aim should be a framework agreement on principles for a future security order, with a commitment to negotiate details after a ceasefire.
brief.argument: The authors largely agree the Abu Dhabi talks produced no breakthrough, but disagree on whether broader talks help Europe or Russia, and on whether pressure on Moscow or a framework deal offers the way forward.
recommendations: Europeans should choose a single representative to speak for them in negotiations.
The United States should move away from a quasi-neutral approach and apply more significant pressure on Russia.
Negotiators should aim for a framework agreement on principles and parameters of a future security order, with a commitment to negotiate details after a ceasefire.

The recent midterm results […]

ai.sum: CFR analysts discuss the US midterm results, the Iran war and a proposed record $1.5 trillion defence budget.

brief.summary: The authors, CFR's Rebecca Patterson and former DIU head Doug Beck, discuss the Trump administration's request for a record $1.5 trillion defense budget against rising U.S. debt and a likely contentious lame-duck session after Democrats take Congress. Beck frames threats in three rings: species-level challenges such as AI, pandemics and energy; a global order under strain from China, Russia, Iran and North Korea, and from transatlantic and alliance doubts; and polarisation within democracies. He argues that the Pentagon rarely starts budget talks by asking what can be cut to fund innovation, and that innovation gets only one to three percent of defence spending. Beck also traces DIU's history and argues that speed, scale and funding flexibility, rather than the top-line number, matter most for rebuilding a ready force.
brief.argument: The authors argue that how the Pentagon spends its budget, especially on rapidly scaling commercial technology, matters more than the size of the top line.
recommendations: Begin budget discussions by identifying what can be cut to free money for reinvestment.
Raise innovation spending well above its current one to three percent share of the defence budget.
Give innovation units funding flexibility, speed and scale authorities rather than only a larger absolute sum.

d576b1d963a7d349.title: New Zealand’s Inconclusive Election Is the Last Thing the Country Needs
d576b1d963a7d349.summary: New Zealand’s politics appear unstable after national elections failed to produce a clear winner. At a time when the country faces severe economic challenges, policy paralysis is a recipe for disaster.

ai.sum: Commentary argues New Zealand's inconclusive national election leaves the country politically unstable amid economic strain.

brief.summary: The author argues that New Zealand's inconclusive national election, with hundreds of thousands of special votes still uncounted, points to a weak and paralysed government at the worst moment. He ties this to the wider fragmentation seen across developed democracies, where the two largest parties recorded their lowest combined share under the current system. He stresses that the Mixed Member Proportional system's low 5 percent or single-seat threshold makes entry easy, so future Parliaments could resemble Israel's unwieldy coalitions. He sets this against economic strain: high living costs, Iran-war fuel price spikes, sluggish growth, falling OECD ranking, high inequality and a brain drain. He concludes that the country may need to rethink its political system.
brief.argument: New Zealand's fragmented, inconclusive election is likely to produce a weak government just as the country faces severe economic and social problems that call for bold policy.
recommendations: Rethink the political system and make major adjustments to it

11e4658df40e588a.title: Hegseth’s Unmaking of the U.S. Military
11e4658df40e588a.summary: Firing admirals and generals, blocking promotions, and gutting DEI programs will hurt recruitment and retention while politicizing the armed services.

ai.sum: Commentary argues Hegseth's firings of senior officers and DEI cuts will weaken US military recruitment, retention and independence.

brief.summary: The authors, through an interview-based podcast episode with two retired flag officers, argue that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's personnel moves are doing serious and lasting damage to the U.S. military. They cite the firing of four-star officers, the blocking or delaying of more than eighty senior promotions (over half affecting women or Black officers), and the attempted elimination of diversity, equity and inclusion programs. The authors contend these steps will hurt recruitment and retention because talented people will leave or avoid hostile institutions, and that repairing a damaged culture takes far longer than destroying it. They also argue the military is being politicised, since officers may now fear that faithfully executing past orders will harm their careers, undermining the principle of loyalty to the Constitution rather than to individuals. The piece frames the concern as one about institutional health and ethos rather than a single policy dispute.
brief.argument: Hegseth's firings, promotion blocks and anti-DEI moves are generationally damaging the U.S. military's talent base and politicising its nonpartisan ethos.

095920fe1dbd2605.title: Moldova cuts energy dependency on Russia with landmark new power line
095920fe1dbd2605.summary: Five years after Russia tried to bring Moldova to its knees through energy pressure, a landmark new power line has removed one of Moscow’s last remaining levers over the country, writes Aura Sabadus. The post Moldova cuts energy dependency on Russia with landmark new power line appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Moldova has commissioned a new power line that removes one of Russia's last energy levers over the country.

brief.summary: The author argues that Moldova's new Vulcanesti–Chisinau power line removes one of Moscow's last energy levers over the country. Moldova had long relied on Russian gas and on the Russian-owned MGRES plant in Transnistria for roughly three-quarters of its electricity, a circular arrangement that also sustained the separatist economy. Since 2021 Moldova has rewired its system toward Europe, synchronised with the EU grid and buying gas across European markets. Electricity from Romania previously still had to pass through the Cuciurgan/MGRES node; the 157 km line lets over half of national consumption, including imports, bypass it. The piece notes the project was more than two years late and that Moldova still needs more domestic generation and further Romanian interconnections for winter reliability.
brief.argument: The Vulcanesti–Chisinau line closes one of the last physical vulnerabilities in Moldova's effort to break Russia's energy grip.
recommendations: Build more domestic generation to reduce reliance on imports.
Complete the two planned Romanian high-voltage interconnections for redundancy and winter supply.

12efa94bbe72b00e.title: The digital yuan is only part of China’s expanding global payments network
12efa94bbe72b00e.summary: Beijing is building multiple layers of financial infrastructure to engage more partners and expand the reach of its renminbi. The post The digital yuan is only part of China’s expanding global payments network appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis says China is building layered financial infrastructure beyond the digital yuan to extend renminbi reach.

brief.summary: The authors argue that China is building several overlapping layers of payment infrastructure rather than relying on the digital yuan alone. Domestically, the PBOC's January rules make retail e-CNY balances interest-bearing deposits on commercial banks' balance sheets, pushing the currency toward "digital deposit money" and away from digital cash, though retail adoption remains weak. Abroad, the authors describe mBridge as a shared-ledger wholesale CBDC project that lost Saudi Arabia, and CBETS as a bilateral bank-to-bank e-CNY link that is easier politically. They also show CIPS expanding its direct participants and volumes, with Iran-related renminbi settlement during the Hormuz disruption as an example of resilience. They conclude that by offering overlapping networks, Beijing gives partners more ways to participate and may gradually reshape cross-border payment infrastructure without displacing dollar networks soon.
brief.argument: China is building multiple interconnected payment layers, including the digital yuan, mBridge, CBETS and CIPS, which together could gradually reshape cross-border payments even without displacing dollar networks soon.
brief.turkey: Turkish banks joining CIPS as direct participants, as the piece notes for Turkey, shows Türkiye is already plugged into this renminbi network.

8fe42c1672df4074.title: What Jensen Huang’s Nvidia exit means for Washington, Wall Street, and Beijing
8fe42c1672df4074.summary: Our experts unpack what the alleged Nvidia espionage incident means for national security, markets, and relations with Beijing. The post What Jensen Huang’s Nvidia exit means for Washington, Wall Street, and Beijing appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council experts assess national security and market implications of an alleged Nvidia espionage incident involving China.

brief.summary: The authors examine the fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation after reports of extramarital affairs, one with a suspected Chinese spy. They argue that Nvidia's chips are central to US leverage over adversary AI progress, so the company's security practices become a single point of failure for export controls. Graham Brookie frames the episode less as an intelligence failure than as a broader coordination and enforcement gap in Washington. Trisha Ray urges direct government oversight, including clearance-like requirements for leadership and security audits tied to export licences. On markets, the authors see instability for Nvidia, which also acts as a financier of AI firms, and note a systemic exposure for the US economy. On China, they judge that Huang's departure removes a key opponent of strict controls, though tougher measures could prompt Beijing retaliation ahead of a Trump-Xi meeting.
brief.argument: Huang's exit exposes Nvidia's security practices as a single point of failure in US AI export controls, opening room for tighter oversight and a more hawkish China policy.
recommendations: Introduce security clearance-like requirements for Nvidia leadership and major customers
Make security audits of exporting entities a precondition for export licences
Use congressional oversight to tighten semiconductor export controls, e.g. the AI Overwatch, Chip Security and MATCH Acts

951a58b1b5174a95.title: Beyond the spy scandal: What the Nvidia-Megaspeed case reveals about export controls
951a58b1b5174a95.summary: Washington must help the private sector protect technology and sensitive information against foreign threats. The post Beyond the spy scandal: What the Nvidia-Megaspeed case reveals about export controls appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis says the Nvidia-Megaspeed case exposes weaknesses in US export controls and protection of sensitive technology.

brief.summary: The authors examine the Nvidia-Megaspeed case as a test of whether US export controls on AI chips can rely on private firms. They describe Megaspeed, a Singapore neocloud that rented Nvidia-powered capacity to Chinese firms and became Nvidia's largest Southeast Asian buyer, with suspicions of physical chip diversion to China that remain unproven. They note that enforcement has been weakened since 2025, with the AI Diffusion Rule reversed and H200 sales to China licensed case by case. Nvidia's voluntary monitoring tools and self-imposed buyer restrictions are presented as insufficient, and firms have divergent incentives. The authors argue that a Democratic-controlled Congress is likely to revive scrutiny, pointing to the Chip Security Act and Remote Access Security Act, and that counterintelligence support for firms in sensitive sectors is needed.
brief.argument: Private firms cannot be relied on to protect export-controlled AI technology, so the US government must tighten enforcement, mandate chip tracking and remote-access controls, and build firms' counterintelligence capacity.
recommendations: Pass the Chip Security Act to require location verification for advanced AI chips before export.
Pass the Remote Access Security Act to give BIS authority over remote access to controlled chips via cloud services.
Hold congressional oversight hearings on Commerce's export-control enforcement and its H200 licensing decisions.
Expand National Counterintelligence and Security Center and FBI outreach to strategically sensitive companies, with Five Eyes partners.
brief.turkey: For Türkiye, the case signals tighter US scrutiny of AI chip flows through third countries such as Southeast Asia, which could affect data-centre and cloud businesses that Turkish firms or hubs may join.

brief.summary: The authors examine the leadership change at Nvidia after Jensen Huang's resignation, contrasting it with Apple's planned succession. Colette Kress, the finance chief, takes over as interim CEO and faces several tests: restoring investor confidence after a roughly 20% share drop, reassuring suppliers such as TSMC and SK Hynix about long-term orders, and repairing Nvidia's strained relations in Washington, where Huang's combative lobbying made enemies. The piece argues that her first test is the 17 November earnings report, and that the hardest challenge is keeping Nvidia central to the AI economy amid rivals such as AMD and in-house chips from cloud giants. The analysis is framed as a corporate governance and market story rather than a policy argument.
brief.argument: Nvidia's interim CEO inherits a dominant but fragile position and must quickly reassure investors, suppliers and Washington while sustaining its AI infrastructure lead.

The background to this shift in emphasis over these vital routes is the patchwork quilt of bitter rivalries that…

ai.sum: Analysis argues that North Africa's land border crossings are increasingly treated as corridors through which regional powers seek to extend influence.

brief.summary: The article argues that power in North Africa and the Sahel now rests less on territory and more on control of transit routes, chokepoints and border crossings. It presents the planned reopening of the Debdeb-Ghadames crossing between Algeria and Libya, due before 2027, as an example: Algeria sees it as an extension of its security perimeter around the Ghadames Basin and as a logistics gateway for state firms such as Sonatrach. Citing political scientist Hamza Berhail, the authors say control of corridors lets actors slow or accelerate flows of energy, trade and supplies. They also point to the Tunis-Ras Jedir corridor and Sahel routes disrupted by coups and sanctions, and to the Atlantic Initiative for landlocked states. The main obstacles they identify are the lack of unified military structures in Libya and the Sahel and the criminal networks that exploit porous borders.
brief.argument: Control of transit corridors and chokepoints has become a functional source of power in North Africa and the Sahel, and the absence of unified security structures leaves these routes open to exploitation.

bba29b6c087f1773.title: Was wäre wenn? RN, AfD und die deutsch-französischen Beziehungen

ai.sum: SWP analyses how a National Rally and AfD government could affect Franco-German relations.

brief.summary: The authors, a German-French working group convened by the Stiftung Genshagen, examine what would follow if the Rassemblement National (France) or the AfD (Germany) entered government. They note that an RN presidency after the spring 2027 elections is a realistic scenario, while the AfD is close to taking a minister-president post in Saxony-Anhalt and has strong polling and a recent win in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Drawing on 14 experts from both countries, the group concludes that either party taking power would mark a turning point, with cooperative logic in bilateral and European relations risking replacement by confrontation. Over the medium and long term, they warn that the foundation of German-French friendship established in 1963 could erode.
brief.argument: Entry of the RN or AfD into power would turn Franco-German cooperation from cooperative to confrontational, threatening the 1963 friendship foundation in the medium and long term.

ai.sum: SWP publishes a paper on Germany and Japan as premium partners moving from alignment to joint action.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Germany and Japan, having styled each other "Premiumpartner", should move from declarations to concrete projects in economic security and defence. They trace the partnership's deepening since 2021 (2+2 format, the secrecy agreement, a dedicated economic-security dialogue) and attribute it to Indo-Pacific and Europe security being intertwined, doubts about US reliability, and weaponised dependencies. On economic security they propose joint critical-raw-materials projects, recycling and stockpiling, and EU-level coordination with Japan, while warning that EU measures such as the Industrial Accelerator Act could disadvantage Japanese firms. On defence they see room for joint development of unmanned systems and possible GCAP participation, enabled by Japan's looser export rules since April 2026, and urge a reciprocal access agreement and space cooperation.
brief.argument: Germany and Japan's partnership has acquired a strategic security dimension and should now turn its political declarations into concrete economic-security and defence projects.
recommendations: Use the planned third round of the economic-security dialogue to identify joint projects on critical raw materials, recycling and stockpiling.
Push at EU level for closer cooperation with Japan on economic security and ensure Japanese firms are treated as trusted partners under the Industrial Accelerator Act.
Pursue joint defence development, especially unmanned systems, and explore a pragmatic route for Germany into GCAP.
Open negotiations on a Reciprocal Access Agreement and expand bilateral space cooperation to security-relevant uses.

7be1ac0a56491fe8.title: Trump Is a Lame Duck. But He’s Still in Charge of U.S. Statecraft.
7be1ac0a56491fe8.summary: Democrats won big, but Congress has little power to check a president who has sidestepped it at nearly every turn. A wounded Trump could make America First statecraft sharper, not softer.

ai.sum: CFR analysis argues that Trump, despite Democratic midterm gains, retains broad control over US statecraft and could sharpen America First policy.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Democratic gains in the midterms will do little to constrain Trump's foreign policy, because Congress has ceded much of its war and statecraft power to the presidency and Trump has repeatedly routed around legislative and judicial limits. They cite the ignored Iran war powers resolution and the Graham sanctions act, which Trump waived while striking a deal with Moscow. They warn that a politically wounded president could sharpen rather than soften America First policy, and that Stephen Miller's appointment reinforces this risk. On Iran, they see a tension between a diplomatic exit, which the midterm losses favour, and a return to military pressure, which Trump's habits make possible. They also expect him to look for a foreign policy win closer to home, with Cuba a possible target. The authors advise Democrats to pursue oversight with sobriety, focusing on Trump-family enrichment, Caribbean and Pacific boat strikes, and deportation policy.
brief.argument: Congress has little leverage over Trump's foreign policy even with a Democratic majority, so America First statecraft is likely to continue and may become sharper, especially if Trump feels politically wounded.
recommendations: Democrats should keep using legislative majorities to constrain Trump but with appropriate sobriety, recognising how hard he is to restrain.

7088e2de594cd6d9.title: The End of Convergence
7088e2de594cd6d9.summary: Why the Developing World Is Falling Behind Again

ai.sum: A CFR piece argues that the developing world is falling behind again, ending earlier convergence.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the developmental model that let late industrialisers catch up over 2000-2015 relied on three forms of arbitrage: cheap labour, access to rich markets and technology, and regulatory slack. All three are now closing at once. Automation has cut the value of low wages, especially in higher-end sectors. Export access, FDI and technology transfer increasingly depend on geopolitics, with export controls and blocs reshaping trade and investment flows. Decarbonisation rules such as the EU's carbon border tax remove the regulatory gap, while most developing states lack the fiscal room to match the subsidies of rich economies. China's overcapacity compresses margins across many sectors. The result, they contend, is a more uneven development geography in which only a few well-placed economies gain, and no clear alternative path to convergence has emerged for the rest.
brief.argument: The developmental ladder that let late industrialisers converge through cheap labour, market and technology access, and regulatory flexibility is closing at once, leaving few alternative routes to convergence.
brief.turkey: For Türkiye, the piece suggests that its manufacturing-led export model faces tighter access to EU and other markets through carbon border rules, technology controls and Chinese overcapacity, with the gains concentrated in a few well-placed connector economies.

92417f8776963504.title: Syria shouldn’t join the Mecca Alliance. It should cooperate with it.
92417f8776963504.summary: Joining the alliance would expose Syria to a new set of threats and increase the chances of regional escalation. The post Syria shouldn’t join the Mecca Alliance. It should cooperate with it. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis argues Syria should cooperate with, rather than join, the Mecca Alliance to avoid new regional threats.

brief.summary: The author argues that Syria should not join the proposed Mecca Alliance, the mutual defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, though it should deepen cooperation with its members. He acknowledges the appeal of collective protection after Israeli strikes and incursions, but contends membership would expose Syria to new threats and make its security depend on Ankara, Riyadh and Islamabad. He also argues that admitting Syria would put the alliance at risk, given Syria's exposed geography and Israeli-Turkish tensions, and could drag Syria into Yemen. He proposes that military training, intelligence sharing, border security, and economic and reconstruction support be pursued through bilateral and multilateral arrangements that carry no treaty obligations.
brief.argument: Syria can secure the military and economic benefits it needs from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan without joining the Mecca Alliance, which would weaken rather than strengthen its sovereignty and the alliance itself.
recommendations: Pursue military training, intelligence sharing, and border security cooperation through bilateral and multilateral channels rather than formal alliance membership
Keep Syria out of the Yemen conflict so its army-building and unified command are not distorted
Use economic integration, investment, and trade corridors to support Syrian recovery without committing Syria to regional wars
brief.turkey: Admitting Syria would deepen Türkiye's strategic link to Damascus but would also commit Ankara to defending an exposed Syrian geography amid Israeli-Turkish tensions, a risk the author says outweighs the gain.

54d1818933328805.title: The election that never happened, and why Washington needs a new strategy toward Nicaragua
54d1818933328805.summary: Nicaragua's dictators called for no more elections, so Washington should call for no more business as usual. It should use targeted economic pressure to push for democratic change. The post The election that never happened, and why Washington needs a new strategy toward Nicaragua appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council argues Washington should use targeted economic pressure on Nicaragua after the regime called off elections.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Nicaragua's indefinite postponement of its November 2026 general election, after a September reform excluding the opposition, marks a turning point that makes business as usual with Managua untenable. They contend Washington should convert its economic leverage, above all its position as Nicaragua's largest export market, into political leverage aimed at restoring democracy rather than rewarding cosmetic concessions. Concrete steps proposed include reviewing CAFTA-DR preferences and targeting regime-linked sectors and firms rather than suspending the whole agreement, which would hurt free-trade-zone workers and regional supply chains. They also call for a clear roadmap tying repression to costs and specified concessions to relief, with off-ramps for lower-level officials, and formal engagement with the democratic opposition at home and in exile. The OAS Ministerial Follow-up Group on Nicaragua is presented as the platform for coordinating these efforts.
brief.argument: Washington should use its trade and economic leverage over Nicaragua, tied to a clear democratic roadmap and engagement with the opposition, to force democratic change after the regime postponed elections indefinitely.
recommendations: Review Nicaragua's CAFTA-DR preferences and target regime-linked sectors and companies rather than suspending the agreement outright
Use Executive Order 14088 to restrict certain imports and investment in specific sectors tied to the regime
Publish a roadmap linking escalating repression to higher costs and specified democratic concessions to sanctions relief, with off-ramps for lower-level officials
Formally engage recognized democratic opposition leaders and organizations, inside and outside Nicaragua, and work through the OAS Ministerial Follow-up Group

74f4665969ba9fc5.title: Same metric, still a mess: The geoeconomics of youth unemployment in China
74f4665969ba9fc5.summary: China is aging too quickly to waste labor, yet it can't generate enough jobs to productively engage its young. The post Same metric, still a mess: The geoeconomics of youth unemployment in China appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analyses China's youth unemployment, arguing rapid aging conflicts with insufficient job creation.

brief.summary: The author argues that China's youth unemployment problem, now around 18 percent among urban 16-24 year olds, is structural rather than cyclical and has become a geoeconomic issue. Peak and trough readings have both worsened since the 2024 metric change, and the author links weak youth absorption to the skills mismatch behind Beijing's strategic industries in AI, electric vehicles and biotechnology. The piece says the jobs shortfall pushes Beijing toward export dependence, which keeps trade tensions with the EU and US high. It also contends that China's shift from infrastructure lending to cheap open-weight AI models changes its influence in the Global South. 3f38adbf7ea8d2fb.title: Washington is reshaping security in North Africa. Congress needs to ask how.
3f38adbf7ea8d2fb.summary: The next US Congress should demand clearer plans from the White House on its Western Sahara and Libya policies. The post Washington is reshaping security in North Africa. Congress needs to ask how. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council urges the next US Congress to demand clearer White House plans on Western Sahara and Libya policy.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Washington is reshaping security in North Africa through two moves that Congress has barely scrutinised: pressing for the closure of the UN mission in Western Sahara (MINURSO), which lapsed after Russia's veto and a failed rival draft, and pushing for a unified Libyan military. On Western Sahara they warn that the ceasefire is now unmonitored and that a unilateral Moroccan move into the former buffer zone could draw in neighbouring states. On Libya they warn that training or equipping units with documented abuses, including support to the Sudanese RSF, would contradict existing US sanctions policy. Their method is oversight rather than a fixed policy position: they ask the administration to set out its plans, risks and benchmarks before funds or waivers are used, and to ensure that Congress sees the rationale in advance.
brief.argument: Washington is taking a more active role in North African security without giving Congress a clear account of its plans, risks or safeguards, so the next Congress should force the administration to justify both policies before acting.
recommendations: Require a report on post-MINURSO ceasefire monitoring, incident communication and US response if forces enter the former buffer zone.
Make RSF support an explicit eligibility criterion for US training and equipment to Libyan units, with waivers reported to committees in advance.
Require a joint State-Defense plan with civilian oversight, vetting, benchmarks and UN-roadmap alignment before new Libyan military integration funds.
Send committee members to Rabat, Algiers and the Tindouf camps to hear the parties directly.
brief.turkey: Türkiye's position in Libya and its ties to Algiers and Rabat are affected by how the US handles military unification and the Western Sahara settlement, and it is a participant in the Libyan unification talks held in Ankara.

2205a2bd7382c874.title: Twenty-Four Hours or Twenty-Four Months: It’s Time for Peace in Ukraine
2205a2bd7382c874.summary: CFR President Michael Froman analyzes this week’s talks in Abu Dhabi.

ai.sum: CFR president Michael Froman analyses this week's Ukraine peace talks held in Abu Dhabi and argues for urgency in reaching a settlement.

brief.summary: Michael Froman, CFR president, argues that the latest Abu Dhabi talks produced no ceasefire or sustainable settlement after nearly five years of war, though restoring direct and military-to-military contact was useful. He says Ukraine has shown flexibility on territory and NATO membership in exchange for credible security guarantees, while Putin still holds maximalist demands despite heavy Russian losses and refinery damage. He notes the U.S. envoys' follow-up trips to Moscow and Dublin, the role Congress could play through the purse, and Europe's push for a seat at the table. He sees the pieces for progress as in place, with the decisive variable being whether Trump can shift Putin's cost-benefit calculation, and concludes it is time to end the conflict.
brief.argument: Progress toward a Ukraine peace now depends mainly on whether Washington can change Putin's cost-benefit calculation, since Ukraine has signalled flexibility and Europe is now involved.
recommendations: Congress should use its power of the purse to fund priorities such as intelligence sharing and Starlink access for Ukraine.
Europe should be included in the next negotiating round, with the Trump administration working with allies.
Washington should apply a mix of sticks and carrots to shift Putin's calculus.
Security arrangements should build on existing European institutions and Cold War-era practices such as OSCE mechanisms.
brief.turkey: Türkiye, as a NATO member with channels to both Moscow and Kyiv and Black Sea interests, has a stake in whether a European security framework for post-war Ukraine takes shape.

abaf0ae33ea061e8.title: Europe Must Step Up to Settle the Russia-Ukraine War
abaf0ae33ea061e8.summary: European leaders must accept that settling the war will mean addressing the broader security order on the continent. Doing so will require finding a clear voice.

ai.sum: A CFR commentary argues European leaders must accept that ending the Russia-Ukraine war means addressing the wider continental security order.

brief.summary: The author argues that a settlement of the Russia-Ukraine war cannot be separated from the wider European security order, which Russia has tied to its war aims since its pre-invasion draft treaties. He holds that European insistence on a ceasefire before any security talks, and Russia's demand that root causes be resolved first, are both untenable. He proposes a framework agreement setting out principles for a future security order, with a credible commitment to negotiate details after a ceasefire. He sees the settlement as defining Europe's geopolitical limits, with the Ukrainian stretch of the border ending NATO's eastward expansion and producing a competitive coexistence with Russia. He stresses that the United States has driven the talks so far, while Europe must agree on a coherent position and a clear representative, since peace cannot be reached without its participation.
brief.argument: Europe must accept that ending the Russia-Ukraine war means addressing the wider European security order, and must settle on a single voice to take part in talks.

804d969f36b4fc26.title: The End of Convergence
804d969f36b4fc26.summary: The first two decades of the twenty-first century saw living standards improve across the developing world. The gap between poor and rich countries, long assumed to be self-reinforcing and perhaps persistent, was apparently closing. Yet today, many less developed countries have no clear ways to industrialize. Joining the global economy does not hold the same possibility of convergence as it used to.

ai.sum: A CFR essay argues that developing countries' convergence with rich economies has stalled and many lack clear industrialisation paths.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the 2000–2015 convergence of developing economies rested on a temporary external environment that now no longer holds. They describe three 'developmental arbitrages' that let late industrializers catch up: cheap labor, access to rich markets and foreign technology, and lax regulation. Each is closing at once. Automation shrinks the value of low wages, Chinese overcapacity and state-led subsidies crowd out entrants, and security-driven export controls and FDI concentration make access conditional on geopolitics. Decarbonization rules such as the EU's carbon border tariffs add to the squeeze. The result, they contend, is a less even geography of development in which only a few well-placed economies gain while most lack a clear route to industrialize.
brief.argument: The developmental arbitrages that enabled the 2000–2015 convergence are closing simultaneously, leaving most developing countries without a clear path to industrialize.

ai.sum: Hudson Institute commentary by Luke Coffey argues the US needs a tailored approach to the Caspian region.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Caspian Sea is a critical gap in US efforts to choke off Iran's sanctioned and military supply lines, since the US Navy cannot operate there as the sea is landlocked. They note that Russia and Iran have used the Caspian for years, that Ukraine and Israel acted on its importance earlier, and that Israel struck Iranian naval assets at Bandar Anzali. They say Task Force Iron Gate must treat the Caspian seriously. Their recommendations are to appoint a special envoy for the region to unify fragmented US policy, to revive a Caspian Guard-style programme that builds maritime security capacity in Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan, and to tailor the approach so regional states are not forced into choosing between Washington and their neighbours Iran and Russia.
brief.argument: The Caspian Sea is an overlooked route for Iranian sanctions evasion and military supply that Washington must address through a bespoke, partner-based approach, since the US Navy cannot operate there.
recommendations: Appoint a special envoy for the Caspian region to serve as a single point of contact and coordinate US policy across agencies.
Revive a Caspian Guard-style initiative under CENTCOM to build maritime security in Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan.
Build on recent US boat transfers to Azerbaijan with maritime surveillance, coastal radar and joint training.
Design the approach so regional states are not forced into an impossible choice between the West and their Iranian and Russian neighbours.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Democratic midterm victory changes the political setting of the US war with Iran without necessarily ending it. A Democratic Congress will scrutinise the war's costs, funding and legal basis, but Trump, who faces no further election, may still prefer a deal he can present as a strategic achievement. The piece says a settlement would require sanctions relief, release of frozen assets and an end to the blockade, and that Congress could make permanent relief harder to deliver. It stresses that Iran's leverage lies in Hormuz, that Tehran's economy is under severe strain, and that the sequencing of concessions remains unresolved. The authors conclude that the White House may favour a narrower deal it can implement through executive waivers, even if this falls short of a lasting settlement.
brief.argument: The midterms make Congressional scrutiny of the Iran war more likely but could also make a lasting Iran deal harder to deliver, pushing Trump towards a narrower, executive-implemented arrangement.

ai.sum: Novelist Eugene Vodolazkin discusses technology and the human spirit in an interview on literature and culture.

brief.summary: In this interview with Al Majalla, Russian novelist and medievalist Eugene Vodolazkin argues that writers shape a people's collective memory more powerfully than historians, since readers keep Tolstoy's version of 1812 even after scholars corrected it. He sees history as a spiral rather than a closed circle, with progress confined to science and technology while the human soul stays the same. He holds that official history often serves present political needs, whereas creative works capture the spirit of an era. He values small sensory details that history drops, and argues that literature comes from gaps, forgetting and room for interpretation rather than from information. He presents his anachronisms in Laurus as symbols of a timeless eternity, and argues that machines can imitate a style but cannot become a writer, so only serious literature will resist AI. His central theme, he says, is time and mortality.
brief.argument: Literature and personal memory, not official history or information, shape how peoples understand their past and what it means to be human, while technology advances but the human spirit does not.

Sometimes, an anonymous email claiming that explosives have been placed aboard a particular aircraft is enough to set off a long and costly chain of events in motion. The airport notifies the airline, the pilot is alerted, airspace is reorganised, and fighter jets…

ai.sum: Al Majalla examines the rising costs of airport hoax bomb threats, which can disrupt flights without any real device.

brief.summary: The authors argue that hoax bomb threats against flights are a cheap but highly effective form of economic sabotage, because the response (diversions, escorts, searches, crew timing breaches, missed connections, airport congestion) costs far more than the threat itself. They point to a November 2026 wave that hit dozens of European flights across at least nine countries, with no explosives found and no attribution established. They caution against quickly assigning political blame, especially amid European concern about Russian hybrid attacks, noting that motives could range from coordinated campaigns to copycats or individuals. They highlight a structural weakness: threats may be received in one country, aircraft cross a third country's airspace, and land in a fourth, so delays in assessing messages add cost. The piece stresses the need for better cross-border information sharing, which the EU activated after the wave.
brief.argument: Hoax airport threats are inexpensive to produce yet impose outsized economic costs, and their fragmented, multi-jurisdictional response exposes a structural weakness that should not be prematurely attributed to a hostile state.
recommendations: Strengthen cross-border information sharing for aviation-security threats
Avoid premature political attribution until investigations are complete
Speed up assessment of threat messages to cut decision-making delays
brief.turkey: Türkiye's major hub airports and its carrier's overflight routes across Europe would face the same cost and coordination exposure if hoax wave campaigns reach the region.

715fdb8a5d3159ac.summary: Why the midterms complicate Trump's search for an Iran deal newspress_en Sat, 11/14/2026 - 04:00 Politics Democratic control of Congress will increase scrutiny of the war and its economic costs, but could also make the concessions needed for a lasting agreement with Tehran more difficult to deliver. The Democrats' sweeping victory in the US midterm elections has changed the political environment in which President Donald Trump is conducting the war with Iran, although it…

ai.sum: Analysis argues Democratic midterm gains will increase scrutiny of the Iran war and complicate any US deal with Tehran.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Democratic midterm victory changes the political setting of Trump's Iran war without fully constraining his military choices. A Democratic Congress will scrutinise the war's costs, funding and legal basis, and could push for an end to the conflict. Yet it could also make a lasting deal harder to deliver, because permanent sanctions relief needs legislative cooperation. The piece stresses Iran's leverage over Hormuz and the economic pressure on Tehran, which has made the sequencing of concessions (blockade lifting versus reopening the strait) a central sticking point. It concludes that a deal relying mainly on executive waivers is more deliverable, but may fall short of Trump's goals and be vulnerable to a future administration.
brief.argument: The midterms increase congressional scrutiny of the Iran war but may make a durable settlement with Tehran harder to implement, favouring narrower executive-based arrangements.
